claims.text: High-temperature exposure of Q235 steel to an aggressive salt environment at 700–900 °C promotes formation of a protective surface oxide layer.
The stability and adherence of the oxide layer govern the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel under high-temperature salt exposure.
A stable, adherent oxide layer mitigates corrosion of Q235 steel.
Instability or spallation of the oxide layer accelerates corrosion.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier to further corrosion.
Oxide-layer spallation exposes fresh Q235 steel to corrosive attack.
Fresh-metal exposure following oxide spallation increases the rate of degradation.
Samples with stable, adherent oxide layers will exhibit lower mass loss than samples with unstable or absent oxide layers.
Samples with stable, adherent oxide layers will retain hardness better than samples with unstable or absent oxide layers.
Q235 steel maintained at room temperature or in a non-salt environment is expected to undergo minimal oxidation and corrosion.
The proposed protective-oxide mechanism is significant only under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures or with different corrosive agents.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome compares stable-oxide samples with samples having unstable or absent oxide, whereas the falsification rule instead requires lower mass change or hardness degradation relative to a room-temperature or non-salt baseline. That baseline is itself described as having minimal oxidation and corrosion, making the expected direction relative to it inconsistent or at least ill-defined.

The mechanism assigns causality to oxide stability and adherence, but the experiment manipulates the entire temperature-plus-salt exposure rather than independently manipulating oxide stability or adherence. Thus the design cannot isolate the claimed governing cause from temperature, salt, atmosphere, or other exposure effects.
